title: The Actor Model
summary: Concurrency via isolated actors that only communicate by message — no shared state, ever. Erlang and Akka are the reference implementations, and 'let it crash' supervision is the model's most senior-level insight.

slides.markdown:
The actor model takes `threads-and-the-shared-memory-model`'s root problem — shared mutable state — and removes it entirely, by construction, not discipline. An **actor** has private state that no other actor can ever touch directly, and the *only* way to interact with it is sending it an asynchronous message.

Erlang (and its VM, BEAM) built its entire concurrency and fault-tolerance story around this model from the start; Akka brought the same idea to the JVM/Scala world. Beyond the concurrency-safety angle, the actor model's **supervision tree** — "let it crash" — is one of the most senior-level ideas in this whole group: instead of trying to prevent every failure, design so failures are contained and recovered from automatically.

slides.subTitle: Private state, message-only communication
slides.markdown:
An actor is a unit of computation with three properties, all of which must hold together for the model to work: it has **private state** nothing outside it can read or write directly; it has a **mailbox** — a queue of incoming messages; and it processes messages **one at a time**, sequentially, never concurrently with itself.

That third property is easy to miss and is actually load-bearing: because a single actor only ever processes one message at a time, its own state is never accessed by two things at once, even though the actor system as a whole is deeply concurrent (thousands of actors all running independently). Concurrency exists *between* actors, never *within* one — which is what makes an actor's internal logic feel like ordinary, sequential, single-threaded code to write.
![Three actors each with private state and an independently processed mailbox](assets/actor-mailboxes.svg)

slides.markdown:
It's worth being precise about what "no shared state eliminates races" actually means, because it's the single most interview-relevant claim in this topic. A lock-based approach *prevents* races only if every developer, on every code path, remembers to acquire the right lock before touching shared state — miss one path, and the bug is back. That's discipline: it works as long as nobody makes a mistake.

The actor model doesn't rely on anyone remembering anything. There is no *syntax* for one actor to directly read another actor's private field — the language/framework simply doesn't offer that capability, the same way Java doesn't offer a syntax to directly execute assembly. A whole bug class becomes not just avoided but structurally unrepresentable, which is a categorically stronger guarantee than "we reviewed the code carefully."

slides.subTitle: "Let it crash"
slides.markdown:
Erlang/Akka's most distinctive idea: instead of writing defensive code to catch every possible error inside an actor, let a failing actor **crash outright**, and have its **supervisor** — a parent actor specifically responsible for it — decide what to do: restart it fresh, restart its whole subtree, or escalate the failure further up.

This sounds reckless until you notice the actual claim: most failures (a malformed message, a transient downstream timeout, a null a developer didn't anticipate) are better handled by *resetting to a known-good state* than by trying to patch around them in place with speculative error-handling code that may itself be wrong. A supervisor restarting a crashed actor with fresh, clean state is often more reliable than an actor that caught the exception and kept limping along in an unknown, possibly-corrupted state.

An actor reference doesn't reveal whether the actor it points to is running in the same process, a different process on the same machine, or on a different machine entirely across the network — sending it a message looks and works identically either way. This is **location transparency**.

The practical payoff: an application can start with all actors local (for simplicity and speed of development) and later distribute some of them across machines for scale — without rewriting the calling code, only the deployment configuration. This is a big part of why Erlang-style actor systems became the foundation of highly available, geographically distributed telecom and messaging systems (Erlang was literally built for telephone switches) — the concurrency model and the distribution model are the same model.

slides.subTitle: The failure mode nobody notices until production
slides.markdown:
The actor model's biggest weak spot: mailboxes are queues, and an **unbounded** mailbox will happily accept messages forever, even if the actor processing them can't keep up. If a consumer actor is slow — a downstream call it's blocked on, a bug making it loop — its mailbox just keeps growing, silently, until memory runs out.

This is a genuinely dangerous failure mode because it hides the actual problem: from the outside, the system looks fine (messages are being "accepted") right up until it isn't (an out-of-memory crash, seemingly out of nowhere). The mitigation is **backpressure**: bounded mailboxes that reject or block new messages once full, forcing the sender to notice and slow down rather than letting the queue absorb an unlimited, invisible backlog. A senior answer to "what could go wrong with actors" names this specifically, not just "actors can crash."

| | Actor model (Erlang/Akka) | Shared-memory threads |
|---|---|---|
| Data races | Structurally impossible — no shared mutable state exists | Possible whenever synchronization is missed |
| Failure handling | Supervision trees, "let it crash" and restart | Exception handling within the failing thread |
| Communication cost | Message serialization/copying overhead | Direct memory access, effectively free |
| Distribution | Same model works locally and across machines (location transparency) | Threads don't cross process/machine boundaries at all |

The bug classes that "disappear entirely" moving to actors: data races and the specific class of deadlocks that come from acquiring multiple locks in inconsistent orders. What doesn't disappear: logic bugs, message-ordering assumptions that turn out wrong, and the mailbox backpressure issue above — the actor model trades one set of failure modes for a different, smaller set, not for zero failure modes.

slides.sectionTitle: Designing a chat room with actors
slides.markdown:
"Design a chat-room service's concurrency model using actors" is answerable directly from what's in this topic:

- **One `RoomActor` per chat room**, holding the room's private state (member list, message history) — no shared mutable room state across the system.
- **One `ConnectionActor` per connected client**, forwarding incoming messages to the relevant `RoomActor` and outgoing messages back to the client's socket.
- **The room's supervisor** restarts a crashed `RoomActor` with a checkpointed member list rather than letting one bad message corrupt the room for everyone still connected.
- **Location transparency** means rooms could later be sharded across multiple machines with no change to how a `ConnectionActor` sends a message to "the actor for room #42" — only the deployment topology changes.

Naming the supervision and distribution angles, not just "one actor per room," is what separates a complete answer from a partial one.

The actor model is one of two "no shared state" answers in this group — `csp-and-channels` is the other, and comparing them directly is worth doing once both are fresh: actors address messages to a named recipient (a mailbox); CSP sends values over an anonymous, typed channel that any goroutine can read from. `comparing-concurrency-models` puts this side by side with threads and async/await against the same design question.
